claims.text: The homogenized HfNbTaTiZr initial state is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy.
Changing the aging temperature induces different degrees of thermal-expansion mismatch among the constituent elements.
Thermal-expansion mismatch generates residual lattice stresses in HfNbTaTiZr.
Residual lattice stresses alter local dislocation-core structures.
Residual lattice stresses modify dislocation-core widths, pinning characteristics, and the effective Peierls barrier.
Lattice-level stress fields arising from mismatch modify dislocation mobility.
The proposed mismatch-induced dislocation mechanism explains the alloy's creep, microhardness, elastic-modulus, stress-strain, and thermoelastic behavior.
Aging treatments that enhance thermal-expansion mismatch within 600–800 °C will increase yield strength relative to an unaged or low-temperature-aged baseline.
Aging treatments that enhance thermal-expansion mismatch within 600–800 °C will increase elastic modulus relative to the baseline.
Aging-induced thermal-expansion mismatch will alter strain-hardening behavior.
Changes in mechanical properties will correlate with XRD-measured lattice-parameter changes indicative of internal stress.
The minimally aged, solution-annealed baseline has lower residual lattice stress from thermal-expansion mismatch than the aged specimens.
The proposed mechanism governs behavior primarily in the 600–800 °C aging window.
At approximately 900 °C, precipitation or other competing phenomena may override the thermal-mismatch mechanism.
Below the aging regime, insufficient residual lattice stress may prevent the proposed mechanism from controlling behavior.
Precipitation or segregation may be difficult to decouple from thermal-mismatch effects without detailed microstructural characterization.
Holding prior deformation history, atmosphere, aging time, and cooling rate constant while varying aging temperature is intended to isolate the aging-temperature-dependent cause.

The hypothesis is falsified if aging at 600–800 °C produces no significant mechanical or lattice-parameter differences from baseline, or if observed changes are attributable solely to precipitation or segregation.
